title: Loading, Hauling, and Tipping
body: Most of the production loss on a shift — backloading, tire damage, a slow cycle — traces back to the same handful of discipline gaps at the loading face and the dump. A crew that keeps spotting, face-loading, and berm discipline tight runs a cleaner, faster cycle without adding a single truck.
keyPoints: Spotting is a fixed sequence, not a guess: single horn means stop, double horn means go, and the bucket position — not the excavator tracks — is the reference the truck reverses to.
Load a straight face, always. Pocket loading is not allowed, and side loading needs written site manager consent plus a risk assessment and supervision — it's an exception, never routine.

Backloading has six known causes: too many trucks for the cycle, poor fragmentation, face cleanup in progress, inconsistent spotting, worn or bare GET, or side/pocket loading against procedure. Diagnose which one before you pull a truck off the face.
No tipping without a berm built to at least half the rear-wheel height. Short berm means no tipping until it's rebuilt — that's the control that stops run-off, not driver judgment.
On ramps and declines: retarder or exhaust brake to hold speed, correct gear engaged, no U-turns except at switchback tires, no parking on an incline unless the truck is broken down.
apply: Walk a loading pad edge yourself rather than trusting the report — the two-meter setback from the crest is an easy one for an operator to creep on over a shift, and it's exactly the kind of gap that doesn't show up until someone's standing there.
